questions.text:
A medical test for a rare disease has the following characteristics:
• The disease affects 2% of the population.
• If a person has the disease, the test correctly identifies them 95% of the time (sensitivity).
• If a person does not have the disease, the test correctly identifies them 90% of the time (specificity).

A person is selected at random and tested. Draw a probability tree diagram and use it to find the probability that the person tests positive.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Correctly sets up probability tree with disease (0.02/0.98) and test result branches. Calculates P(positive) = 0.02 × 0.95 + 0.98 × 0.10 = 0.117. Merit: Shows clear working with all probabilities labelled on the tree. Excellence: Full solution with clearly communicated reasoning.

questions.text: Given that the person tests positive, find the probability that they actually have the disease. Show your working clearly.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Identifies this as a conditional probability problem. Merit: Correctly applies Bayes' theorem or reads from tree: P(D|+) = 0.019/0.117 = 0.162. Must show the formula or clear reasoning from the tree. Excellence: Provides correct answer with clear communication about why the probability is surprisingly low despite the test's accuracy, linking to the low base rate of the disease.

questions.text:
A health official claims: 'Since the test is 95% accurate for detecting the disease, a positive result means you almost certainly have the disease.'

Comment on this claim, using your answers to parts (a) and (b) to support your reasoning.
questions.expectedAnswer: The claim is incorrect. While the test correctly identifies 95% of people WITH the disease, a positive result only means about a 16.2% chance of actually having the disease. This is because the disease is rare (2%), so most positive results come from the large number of healthy people who get false positives. The official is confusing P(+|D) = 0.95 with P(D|+) = 0.162.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: States the claim is not correct. Merit: Explains that the probability of having the disease given a positive test is only about 16%, using their calculation. Excellence: Clearly explains the base rate fallacy — that because the disease is rare, the false positives from the 98% without the disease overwhelm the true positives. Distinguishes between P(+|D) and P(D|+) in context.

questions.text:
A two-way table shows the results of a survey of 200 Year 12 students about their preferred study method and whether they achieved Merit or Excellence in their last exam.

|              | Merit/Excellence | Not Merit/Excellence | Total |
|--------------|-----------------|---------------------|-------|
| Group study  | 42              | 38                  | 80    |
| Solo study   | 36              | 84                  | 120   |
| Total        | 78              | 122                 | 200   |

Calculate the probability that a randomly selected student from this survey prefers group study AND achieved Merit or Excellence.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Correctly calculates 42/200 = 0.21 (or 21/100). Must show the fraction or calculation, not just the answer.

questions.text: Are the events 'prefers group study' and 'achieved Merit or Excellence' independent? Justify your answer with calculations.
questions.expectedAnswer: P(Group) = 80/200 = 0.4, P(M/E) = 78/200 = 0.39. If independent, P(Group AND M/E) = 0.4 × 0.39 = 0.156. Actual P(Group AND M/E) = 42/200 = 0.21. Since 0.21 ≠ 0.156, the events are NOT independent.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Calculates at least two of the required probabilities. Merit: Correctly compares P(A and B) with P(A) × P(B), or compares P(A|B) with P(A). Concludes they are not independent with correct justification. Excellence: Clear, well-communicated solution with all working shown and a contextual conclusion.

questions.text: Calculate the relative risk of achieving Merit or Excellence for group study compared to solo study. Interpret your answer in context.
questions.expectedAnswer: Risk for group study = 42/80 = 0.525. Risk for solo study = 36/120 = 0.3. Relative risk = 0.525/0.3 = 1.75. Students who prefer group study are 1.75 times as likely to achieve Merit or Excellence compared to students who prefer solo study.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Calculates at least one of the risk values correctly. Merit: Correctly calculates relative risk = 1.75 and interprets in context (group study students are 1.75 times as likely to achieve Merit/Excellence). Excellence: Adds a caveat that this is an observational study so we cannot conclude group study causes better results.
